blocks.x: George Brunus The Musical Brunus Family It's going okay.

Good morning ladies and gentlemen. This is George Brunus of the Musical Brunus Family of New Orleans. It's a little in the view, the gentleman would like to know, I was born New Orleans, the Irish Channel, February 6th, 1902. I'm now 56 years of age, going pretty strong for my age. I came up from New Orleans. There was a telegram sent by a drummer that came up here first, Rag Baby Stevens. He was working at a place called the Campbell Gardens on Campbell and Madison and he sent me a wire for my brother Albert, known as Abby, for him and I to come up and join his band. Abby was leery, he didn't want to walk across Ty's back and I was afraid to leave town, I was afraid of getting stranded. So I took it over to a friend of mine, Paul Moraes, whose father was in the fur business. Whose brother now runs the Jazz Southland label in New Orleans, on St. Louis Street. So I says, Paul, Abby don't want to go to Chicago. I says, I'm kind of leery, I'm afraid. Paul says, man, give me that wire. He says, I'll go. So Paul went up and introduced himself to Rag Baby Stevens and Rag Baby liked him. And then I waited a while and Paul got the railroad fare from his father and sent me $60. I took my little mackinac, my cap and my cowlick and my horn and a piece of paper, newspaper. I didn't have a trombone case then. I had bought it in the hock shop. And I came home to Chicago, went to the Campbell Gardens that night. And me being from New Orleans, I didn't know such thing of snow. So we played the first set. Rag Baby and Paul. And there was a, I just can't recall the piano player's name now. And then we had, who was playing clarinet? So far back, that's a long time ago.
Somebody from Chicago?

Uh, Rag Baby, Paul, myself and Tramonist, piano player. I just can't recall the piano player. Oh God, yeah. So, uh, we played the first set and went over pretty good and ragged. And the boss, uh, Stein was very happy. So I happened to go outside and somebody said, it's snowing. So I wanted to see snow and it was snowing like the diggings. You've never seen it before. I never seen it. I've seen it on Christmas cards, but I thought it was fictional. So I start rolling around in the snow and clowning and throwing snowballs, never having a ball. So the boss comes on and he says, you're on. I says, to hell with the job. I says, I quit. I didn't have a dime in my pocket. I was so happy. So the guy says, well, all right, have a little fun and then come in and play. So I missed the set and I went back in. And then from that time on, the job was all right. We stayed there all for a good length of time. And then we went to a place called the Lincoln Gardens. And, uh, well, I'm getting a little ahead of my story. When I first came in, uh, uh, after the, uh, what's the name? We went down to Blatt's Palm Garden. That's where I met the famous Jack Pettis on the, on the C. Miller saxophone, Frank Snyder, and Elmer Schoble. And then Muggsy could only play one tune at that time. A number called Sensation. So these two racketeers, uh, bouncers and hoods, they, uh, after, uh, Jack and, uh, Elmer introduced Muggsy and I. I played, Muggsy sat in, we played. So after this, after the night was over, they took us over to an athletic club. And they made us put the boxing gloves on. I said, man, I don't want to hurt this man. I just met him. I just said, hello, how do you do this? So they made us do it. You know how they do in Chicago. They made us do it. So we boxed for about two hours. I knocked Muggsy down. Muggsy knocked me down. I got a broken thumb. I broke on Muggsy's head. Then Muggsy sprang out and he went with, uh, Miller's Black and White Melody Boys. And that's when, after we played the Lincoln, we went, after we played the Camel Gardens, we went to the Lincoln Gardens on Lincoln and Madison. That's where, uh, Pettis got the, uh, idea. He didn't get the idea. There was a telegram sent to go to work on the Streckfus boats in St. Louis. There was, uh, what's the Clannet players? Uh, um, Palazano. Oh, yeah.
I know who your name is.

Oh, he's from New Orleans. Well, it was Paul Morais, myself, and, uh, Jack Pettis, and the rest of the boys were from, uh, St. Louis. So we went down there, we got the job on the boat, and we lived on the boat, and, uh, Tony Palazano. Yeah, something like that.
I know, I know.

Well, he's now with the syndicate, I think, uh, dealer or something. So we got down there a while, and then we hit Davenport, and Rap was going with a young lady down there, and he come in and sat on the boat one night. So the manager, the, Captain Byrne, that's the captain of the boat, the, uh, the, uh, it was the, uh,
The Breakfast Line, huh?
Yeah. The St. Paul? No, the, uh,
The Sydney? Let's see.

Uh, I think it was the Sydney. The JS? No, the JS was turned into the Sydney. It is. Yeah, that's it. It was the JS. So, uh, Rap Poli got the job. They let Palazolo go, and, uh, Tony Palazolo, I think that's his name. So, uh, Rap joined the band, and then we, that's where I met Black, the banjo player, and, uh, Bix used to come out and, uh, sit in. It was from Davenport, and, well, he was a great trumpet player. God bless him. And, uh, then from the boat, we'd, uh, we got the offer to come into Friars Inn.
Well, can you tell me a little bit about Rap? Had he been, uh, living in Davenport, working on a boat, or what?
Well, he was working in Davenport somewhere, and he was going with this young, beautiful, blonde girl, and, uh, she, I think she was killed in an automobile accident.
Well, do you remember something about, uh, B. Palmer, too? Oh, well, that's the... She had brought him up or something, do you remember?

Yeah, that's right. B. Palmer, and it was Santo Picora, who is now at the, uh, famous door. Emmett Hardy on trumpet, there was the trumpet boy. Uh, Leona Paula, Frisco on drums, no, Martin Burke on drums, and, uh, Al Siegel on piano. And she had a shimmy act that went out in vaudeville, and it was a wonderful act. And, uh, then Rap, uh, that, that thing broke up. It lasted a pretty good long time, a couple of years on the off-room circuit. And then Rap left, and that's when we, when we got him in, uh, Davenport. And then we left the boat, and then we went, we got the offer to go into Fryers Inn. And the, uh, the first band to go into Fryers Inn was, uh, Paul Merez, Leon Rapola, Elmer Schoble on piano, uh, Frank Snyder on drums, uh, Louis Black on banjo, who was now a police officer in Davenport, I think. And, uh, Steve Brown. No, it was Arnold Lake Canna first. And then that band split up, and Elmer went out to the Midway, oh, we were there for three years, I think. No, two years. Elmer went out to the Midway Gardens with his own band, and Snyder left and went somewhere, I don't know where he went, and, uh, let's see. We, we got, uh, Mel Stitzel on piano. Yeah, with Captain Daniel.
Uh, was, uh, Mike Fritzel, the, uh, boss, uh? Yeah, that's right, that's right. You don't have to lean over close to the dingus. No. You don't have to talk right at that, that'll take a moment.

We replaced, uh, Frank Snyder with Ben Pollack, and we replaced Elmer Schoble with Mel Stitzel on piano, then we replaced Arnold Lake Canna with Steve Brown, who to me was the world's greatest jazz bass player. In fact, he started all these guys slapping a bass. No. And I think he's now Secretary of the Union in Detroit.
Yes, he's an officer there.
So, uh, then we went on.
Can you tell me about, uh, Pollack? You say he wanted to sit in, what was that story?

Oh, that was, uh, when, one time he used to hang around the Friars a lot. In fact, uh, Benny Goodman, all the kids were going to Austin High School, and they used to, couldn't come in, so they'd sit on the outside and listen. So one time, uh, he heard, Benny heard his, Pollack heard his, uh, talking about Snyder, couldn't make it, and he walked up to me and he says, uh, do you mind, Mr. Bruins? He says, if I sit in, I says, uh, how do you play? He says, oh, he says, I play pretty good. I says, well, all right, sit in. I says, but don't give me no fancy damn beats. Just hold a good New Orleans Dixie beat. So he sat in and then he made good from then on. We liked him. And he was the first guy that I ever see do, uh, what, the silver dollar or the key on the cymbal? Where he go, boom, chhh, chhh, chhh, and we roll the cymbal. Now they all doing it now. So, uh, we stayed there and we went out to a place called the Midway Garden. Oh, excuse me for interrupting.
What kind of a place was Fires in? Was it in the basement?

It was in the basement on Wabash and Van Buren. It was owned by Mike Fritzl alone. No syndicate, no Jacobson. And, uh... Were there a lot of gangsters around? A lot of hoods in those days. Can I mention the names? Uh, yeah.
We could cut out anything.

Terry, Droogan, Frank Lake, Schema, Drusie, uh, Nails Martin. It was a place where the boys hung out and it was, uh, it was run pretty nice. There was never any trouble. And they had, uh, men entertainers and girl entertainers would go out and spread after the set and sing to each table. They'd sing, uh, Ace in the Hole and, uh, what's this other thing? It was a Tart song. Oh, it made a million dollars. Frankie and Johnny and all those songs. It's the good old days. What were your hours?
How long did you play there?

Well, we went to work at, uh, well, we'd switched. First we went to work early, then we'd switch and went to work late. We'd get in there about, uh, ten o'clock. We'd be, we'd first, we'd went from eight until, uh, two. Then it changed the hours. The business picked up so good that we started going into ten and going through four and five in the morning. That's when we used to get good overtime. We made good money there. So then, that band broke up after so long, of time, and then, uh, I get the job at the Valentino Inn, which was on Adams Street, was owned by Dan Barone. And then, uh, I had Kyle Pierce on piano, Caffarelli on, uh, Gene Caffarelli on trumpet, Bill Paley on drums, uh, Dale Skinner on saxophone, and I sent to New Orleans for Chink Martin on bass. And, uh, we stayed there. We played up in the balcony, and we stayed there a while. And they used to do a couple of shootings in there, federal men shooting, uh, uh, bootleggers. So then, one night, Ted Lewis walked in. He says, boy, he says, I want you for my band. I says, well, Mr. Lewis, I says, I'm working here. I'm a leader. He says, well, he says, come down and have an audition for me. So he was at the Apollo Theater now, which is known as the, uh, uh, It's the United Artists now, isn't it? Maybe, I'm not sure. Yeah, that's now known as the United Artists' Theater. And it was with a thing called the, uh, 1923 Passing Show. So I go down there, and there's about 25 trombone players sitting there. So the tune called, uh, Dreamy Melody was popular then, and, uh, me, I was playing the Tiger X 40 times a night. So he asked me to audition. I played a solo, Pretty Melody, uh, Dreamy Melody, and he liked it. And we played the St. Louis Blues, not his arrangement, but, and we played Tiger X. So he come over, he says, listen, bub, he says, the job is yours. He says, but I have to show courtesy to these other boys. He says, I have to listen to them. He says, but the contract is yours. So I went out, and that's when my, at that time my brother Henry, who was to me the world's greatest trombone player, God bless him. And my brother Merritt, when we left the Fry's Inn, I called my brother Merritt and tried to get Chris Mann's band from the Plantation Hollywood, and they had a big band. So Mike heard the band over the phone, he liked it, and then Chris Mann didn't like Chicago, so my brother took the band over Merritt. And Merritt and Henry had the band. So after I went back and told them the news that I got the job at Lewis, I was broke as usual, and, uh, I said, look, I need some money. I said, man, these guys must be sharp guys on Broadway. They walked down the street, they said, here goes Ted Lewis's band. I went out and brought a, brought a derby hat and a beautiful brown top coat and pair of shoes and spats and everything. I want to look like a Broadway guy. So when I walked in there, I go back to the dressing room, I said, man, this is that famous Ted Lewis band. Look at this room, look how these guys live. So that all went by. So the first day I get on the stage with Ted, I've never been on the stage before and I was nervous. And all the girls were, the chorus girls were feeding me mint, you know, to keep my mouth wet. So Ted gets a wire. My mother died in the war. So, uh, I was broke. So Ted knew it all through the show and he let me finish the show. So after the show, he says, son, he says, I got some bad news for you. He says, uh, your mother passed away. So I go into it and he says, what are you going to do? He says, you want to go home? I says, well, I'm kind of short on a little money. I'm still losing. He's peel out $200. He says, here, this will get you home. He says, if you want to come back, he says, let me know. So my brother, brothers and I, we got together and went down for the funeral. And then after my mother, they buried my mother, I came back up and I've been, I've stayed with him for 17 years, off and on, you know. Yeah. Yeah. So then we traveled here, we traveled to Europe, we traveled all over. We had Jimmy Dorsey one time and Don Murray, who was a great saxophone. Both of them were great. And, uh, we made some records with, uh, Benny Goodman, Fats Wara, some of the finest records Lewis made.
How long was Muggsy with you there too?

Uh, I got Muggsy with Lewis. He was with Lewis for about seven years. He was with, uh, Ray Miller's band down the, uh, Sherman. And I went to him and I says, uh, I told Lewis, I says, I got a good man down there, Sherman. He says, well, if you recommend him, he must be good. He says, I'll take him without hearing him. I says, oh, no. I says, you're going to hear him first. He says, I don't want me taking him. So Muggsy auditioned for him and he liked Muggsy. Muggsy stayed with him for seven years. And, uh, then what happened, let me see, uh, well off and on, then I went to New York. And I stayed in New York. I was running for a couple of weeks and I changed my name. I didn't change the name, but I went to numerologist. Yeah. This, uh, Garen Moore. And, uh, he told me that he changed my name. He took a couple of letters out. Instead of spelling it G-E-O-R-G-E, he spelled it G-E-O-R-G and instead of B-R-U-N-I-E-S, he put it B-R-U-N-I-S, which means the way he had it would be successful in the amusement field, which it was, has been. It has changed me. Of course, I made the money. I'm broke, but I still made money. It's not nobody's fault that I throw the money away. So, then I, uh, I defied myself. You know, it's Friday the 13th. I'm walking down Broadway and things are rough. After I left Louis for two or three weeks, I was living at the Palace Hotel on 45th Street, so I says, I'm gonna defy. It was Friday the 13th. I walk under a ladder. A black cat crossed me. And there was something else happened. I says, I'll either do or die. That afternoon, about five or six o'clock, I go home. There's a call for me to go to work at Nick's in Greenwich Village. There's a recording date for me. And everything happened. So I call up Nick and I says, we got Sharky. Would you like to go to work with Sharky? I says, what's the money? What's the price? Everything was agreed. So we went to Nick's, uh, Corners down there, the old place.
I remember that.

So, uh, the band was pretty good. We were supposed to make a picture and, uh, for Damsel in distress, distressed with, uh, Ginger Rogers and Fetist there. So a little argument came up between Sharky and I, and I told Sharky to go. I didn't want to go. So then we, we stayed there, gradually against each other. And, uh, Nick made enough money there to build a new place across the street, which was 1937, December 10th. I'll never forget it because Red McKenzie was almost killed with a cab. We were carrying the tables across, you know, in the morning. We were drinking all the beer and helping them move. So I stayed at Nick's for 10 years. I was a house man down there. Every band came in there. Once I was a leader and I'd play with another band and I'd become a leader again. Bobby worked for me. I worked for Bobby. Pee-wee worked for me. I worked for Pee-wee. Same person. I would just switch it around. And we did terrific business. So then I leave there and I go with Miss Mills Calvacate, a girl and boy band. And Mills was booking me. Uh, in the meantime, I had met a man that's becoming very popular now. Miss Keely Smith's husband, uh, Louis Prima. Uh, he came up. When I was going good at Nick's, uh, he came up in New Orleans. He made a batch of records. He didn't know anybody. So he'd wake me up at nine o'clock in the morning and, uh, get me to go around to the agent's office. And I said, the agents knew me, but they knew in the back, but they didn't want to talk to Prima. They heard Prima played like Louis Armstrong. And I said, if they wanted the original, they'd get the Armstrong. Why get an imitator? So then I get an idea, a job for, through, uh, Cole and Lenny Hayton. I think there was three musicians on the Famous Door. So they'd come to me and ask me to get a band. They wanted a suitcase and whisper room with a wow-wow trombone. They wanted crazy effects, the sounds. So I said, well, I got just a guy for you, Louis Prima. So we had Prima and a piano player from New Orleans and, uh, Adams, Mike Adams was killed on the guitar. And this Ryan used to be with Jimmy Dorsey on bass. So we'd go and then we'd pack the joint. So I used to play a lot of bass notes and this arranger used to come in there. He was a big man, Gordon Jenkins. And he'd sit alongside of me and I'd play them low notes. He says, uh, hey, Bub, he says, can those things be arranged? I says, I don't know. You're an arranger. You should know that. I says, I'm just playing them. It's up to you to get them on the paper some kind of way. So Prima and I got into a little swivel and, uh, I went to Cole and I says, look, there's no use to working with this guy. I says, uh, I'm detracting from the guy and he don't like it. So Prima goes up and he says, I don't want to work with Broomers. He's detracting from me. I says, you're just two minutes too late, boy. I'll just quit you. I says, this was my job. Remember that. I gave it to you. This was supposed to be Brunus and his sextet. So then we caught it.
Did you make records with Prima from other students?
Yeah, we made, yeah. In fact, they just released one where I was a side man. Now I'm the leader and Prima's a side man. The same record. It's bootleg.
Oh, I saw that thing. Yeah.
Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. That's it.
Yeah, on some of that, the cheek labels.

And then I still went back. I was down at Nick's. In and out, in and out, in and out. So, uh, then I leave there. After I leave the Mills Cavalcade, uh, I went to Jimmy Ryan's for five and a half months. Did a terrific job there, thank God. And then, uh, I went down to Connors, and Connors was a little bit under the red side. And Pete Pesky asked me if I'd go to work for him. And I says, well, he says, you did a good job up at Ryan's, I hear. Well, I think I made about $55,000 with Jimmy Ryan in five months. It's not bad for a small place. Mm-hmm. So they were putting different exits and everything. The police were there every day, and the firemen. Yeah. So when I decided, I told, uh, I says, except the Condon, I says, I don't think Condon wants to work with me or something like that. So he says, look, I run this place. He says, I'll take that name down and put your name up there. This is true.
Is this the new Condon's over there on?
No, this is the old one in Greenwich Village.
Greenwich Village there.
47 West 3rd Street.
Yeah, that's what I'm in. I mean, after, yeah, that's what I said.

So, uh, Bill Davis' wife run up, and when she found out, she says, oh, my Bill's got to work with Brunus. So, uh, Bobby Hackett was staying at the bar, and we were talking Condon, Pesky, and so Condon says, well, he says, I got to do something I never did in my life. I hate to do it. I got to fire two guys. I think it was Brad Gowns and, uh, Max Kaminsky. So, uh, he says, I got to put Barnum and Bailey in there. So Bobby Hackett says, look, no matter who you're putting in, as long as you do business, he says, Brunus can do business. I'll pay for you. So I went in, I stayed there three years, and I run up a tab, I think, of $1,200. Hey! So, uh, then I got an offer to go out to, come out here to Chicago to, uh, the Sky Club. It wasn't much, it was a nice place, but they never advertised, and I had, uh, the, uh, high school kids, uh, what's the name of the high school? I had, uh, Scarsdale High School kids. I had Jimmy, Johnny Glazell, uh,
Bob Wilbur, is he with you?

No, I had, uh, Harry Green on clarinet, and his drummer that plays like Buddy Rich, what's his name? Well, I just can't remember. Anyway, I'm sure you work all over there. Most of the guys, uh, most of the guys were at the, uh, Rhymes. So we came out here, and we stayed, uh, we were supposed to be there two weeks, and we stayed six months. And at the weekends, it was beginning to pick up mouth-to-mouth publicity. So then I got an offer to go into the Blue Note. And just then, the band quit me, went back to New York. They went, they didn't like Chicago. So, Mr. Holstein hired the band on the strength of the band, you know, on the strength of the band I had. So, I had to pay their fare back. There's a union rule that if a musician quits, he pays his own way back. But I was stuck. The union stuck me. I had to pay their fare back. So, I went down to Blue Note, and I told Mr. Holstein, I says, I haven't got the same band. He says, well, I gotta get somebody in there. I went down to the union, and I got four or five guys, and it was nothing like the band I had. So, I got up and said to the first night, I said, ladies and gentlemen, this is not the band I had at the Sky Club. Holstein says, don't ever do that, he says. Don't ever say that to an audience. I said, well, look, I don't feel right. I can't play with these guys. I never played with them. I don't know what they're like. So, we battled through, I think, two weeks. So, then, I went back in again with Hodes and Lee Collins, and stayed there 14 weeks. And then I went back again with, in the meantime, I went over to the Jazz Limited for 12 weeks. And I worked there 12 weeks, and it was too quiet for me. I couldn't take that, so I checked out there and went back into Blue Note again. Then I went back again for six more weeks with Slim Gaylord and the old Smokies, what do you call those? That seven, the Weavers.
Oh, yeah.
They sold a couple of million records. And then from there, I went into the Brass River for three weeks with Schwartz, and that's when the 11-11 come and got me.
What year was that?
Oh, I went in there at 50... What was it? 52?
No, before that.
I know it was June the 6th, because it was on Ted Lewis' birthday. I think it was 50 or 51.
You've been there about seven years.

Yeah, I'm going on eight now, yeah. It was about 50 or 51. I know it was June the 6th. And then I left the 11-11, and I went out to the Red Arrow for three months. Did very good out there. Came back. Then I went out to the TomTom with Danny Alvin for three months. Did very good out there. And then came back to the 11-11. And I left there and went to the Preview for three months, and here I am back again.
Well, some of the old... Did you ever go to Europe?
I was three times with Ted Lewis.
Ted Lewis. What countries did you visit, do you remember?

France, England, Belgium. We played the... I stand Belgium. We played the L'Ambassadeur in Paris. We played the La Apollo. They called it the Apollo. La Apollo, they say over there. And we played in London. We played the Hippodrome and the Kit Kat Club.
Did Ted Lewis feature you much in solos and special numbers?

I used to sit down front. I used to use the first wow-wow mute ever made that Patty Harmon made. And he'd say, play me rhythm, Brunus. Give me rhythm. And I'd just have to hold the thing choked and pump out rhythm.
That was the regular Harmon mute then.
Yeah, it was the first one ever made. Patty Harmon gave it to him. He ran a dance hall. That's where Louie and Joao used to play.
Oh, is that the same Harmon mute? I thought it was the manufacturer.
No, that's... Harmon's dreamland. That's right. That's the guy who invented the wow-wow mute. I didn't know. I see.
There's some stuff you were wondering what to talk about. I never knew that in all my life.
I still got the mute. It's all batted up, but it's over at the level.
You have a little hole in the front that you can use your hand.
Yeah, it looked like a cuspidore.
Yeah. Yeah, that's it.
And...
While we were talking about those different effects, did you ever use old things like derbies or the plunger?

Oh, yeah, yeah. I used a plunger on a record. I think it was Muggsy's Lonesome Road. People wrote in the crystal. What is that instrument on there? They didn't know it was a trombone. It was on Lonesome Road. And then Muggsy and I used to do a lot with Ted Lewis, and then we'd take the hats with that. Well, a lot of big bands are doing that now.
Tell me about back in New Orleans when you were a kid. Did they use anything? Some people said they used sugar cans or buckets and things over. What did you use?
Well, molasses cans, anything. Anything about this high.
About a seven, eight inch high.
Anything, a derby. Dave Kline used to use the electrolyte bulb with tape on it. He used to do the taps with Ted Lewis, a beautiful effect from the distance.
Who did that?
Dave Kline. He is now a big man in California. Got all the contracts out there for the jingles and things, gimmicks.
Yeah. Did you ever use a bottle inside? I've seen people do that.
Use a bottle or use a record?
A phonograph record?
Yeah. Let it loose and it vibrate.
Right up against the bell.
Yeah.
Well, we're on there.
Now, Nappy over at 11-Levelin is using the plant as peanut can.
Yeah. Can you tell me about your horn? What kind of a horn do you use now? What make is it and how big a...

Well, the first horn I had I bought for $3 in the hawk shop. And then I got this thing. This thing is about... I had it overhauled once. I sent it back to King. It's the King H.N. White in Cleveland. I sent it back once and the guy knew me. He says, where'd you get this horn, Bruno? It's from Methuselah? It was all beat up. But they fixed it up good and they lacquered it.
The same horn you have?
Yeah, it's about... How old is it? Oh, about... 40... 47 years.
Really? It looks good.

Well, I had it fixed up. My brother Henny played a Holton boy and he had adhesive tape and everything and the holes and the slide and everything. There was the boy that played trombone when she was living. Oh, God.
Can you tell me a little bit more about him?
All that stuff I do is for my brother Henny. That playing with the foot and Mike Ratton and all those guys are getting credit. My brother was the first one to do that.
That's what I knew.
My brother played bass on a little stool when he was a kid, my brother Henry.
String bass.
Yeah. I think my brother Abbey's got pictures of that yet.
Didn't see that.

And there's a guy who can put a trombone in one position and play like the guy playing the bugle and all. Play the national anthem in one position with a control of the lip he had. Right there. And all that stuff, playing with the foot and that marching around and the saints, all that stuff, my brother did that before any of those guys. Yeah. Now the Dukes and everybody's getting credit for stuff we did. I played in Tom's Roadhouse, posed as a midget. I'm putting black wrinkles in it. The cops says, get that school boy out of here. He's not a school boy. He's a midget. He's 32 years old. Oh, we did a lot of stuff. New Orleans was a crazy town. It's fabulous. Yeah, that's right. We got a lot of money.
Can you tell me some more about your home when you started? Your father and the rest of your family, what they played?
Well, there was Richard and my two late brothers Henry played trombone. My brother Rudy, he was the last one, Barrett. He was 70 years old. He played bass fiddle.
And Rudy was the oldest in the family.

Yeah. And he was a brewmeister. No, Richie's after, before. And Rudy was a brewmeister in the New Orleans Brewing Company. And then there was Henry, then there was Merritt, and there's Albert and myself, and my brother Richard, the four of us are living here. And my sister and my mother, they played guitar, both guitar and piano. And my old man would get us out after dinner and make us all. We had Abby, Merritt, and Richie on trumpets, and my brother Henry on the trombone, and I played the upright alto. I was playing the upright. That was my first instrument. When I saw Henry play the trombone, I drooled, and I threw the alto away and wanted to play trombone. And then my sister, my mother, and he'd get there with the violin, play the mockingbird when the maple leaves were falling, and we'd start playing so nice for a couple of, give me kicks, and we'd start jazzing up. He'd run the hell out of it and throw the violin down. He says, you little jazz damn fools, he says.
So did you really play out there almost every night on the-

Well, no. When he felt in the mood, if he didn't eat too much, he'd say, all right, boys, get the instruments, and we'd have to be there. And I'll guarantee you, it's not like today. At nine o'clock, we hung out when we were playing music. Papa Lane used to pick me up, see? I played with his Reliance band, and he'd pick me up and we'd play the dance, and we'd get fifty cents an hour, Crescent Park, Owls Halls, Suburban Park, Elvira Park, and Algiers, and we'd play the parades. But he'd pick me up, and he'd take me to the job, and if it was too far away from my house, I'd sleep at his house, see?
Yeah.

And then he'd bring me home the next day, and he'd give my mother the money, and my mother would give me a dime to go get a piece of candy or something. And at nine o'clock, and we weren't working, when that market bell rang, boy, I had to be in there at nine o'clock, he'd be behind the door, he'd bring us with a baseball bat. And there's seven of us, and thank God, there's none of us stepped outside the law in there. And the kids today, boy, we, I advise kids to take musical instruments up and keep away from those guns.
Keep away from guns.
I got a boy up in Evanston, we're met now, he lives, and his name is Bobby Wright, and he's a wonderful boy, he's very good at school, his gradings are good.
Oh, I know him, played piano.
Yeah, I played with the Storyville 7, a bunch of kids.
Does he play with the trombone, how, too?

In two years, that kid accomplished, and I'm telling you, you can close your eyes, he sits in at the 11-11 with me, and people rave about him. I introduce him as my son. Oh, he's, that's... He's 17 now.
He doesn't register on me.
Bobby Wright, the piano player, aren't you? Yeah, he played with the Storyville 7. Oh, sure. You should hear that kid play trombone.
Trombone, he was just...

You close your eyes, you'll sweat, and he does the finger gag, and the time gag, and the drink gag, and everything. People say, you gotta go. I says, well, after he gets through playing, I say, now, ladies and gentlemen, I can die happy. There's somebody who sounds like Brunus, and at least I'm dying, and I know he hasn't got a gun in his hand.
Did you give him lessons, or did you...

No, I showed him a thing. He just bought my records, and he'd call up his dad. His dad come in and says, why don't you adopt this boy? He'd buy the records, and go home, and sit down, and play with him. He's real jazz enthusiasts. He don't like...
He's real jazz and through jazz. He don't like bebop and he don't like none of the others. He's strictly...
I knew him when he played piano real well too. He started out on ragtime.
He was over at a club last Friday night, him and his mother.
Oh, I wish I'd been there.
How long are you going to be in town?
Tomorrow. I leave tomorrow.
I was going to say, I'd have him come in there and play for you.
I'd have been up to their home when they'd have sessions.
Oh, we had some great sessions up at his house. There's another little kid I got in.
Okay, it's going. Does this kid play, Bobby Wright play by ear?
He knows music. He knows music. He studied piano music.
Yeah, I knew he studied some piano.

And there's another kid I got. He's 14 or 15 now. Jimmy Butler up in Columbus, Indiana. We had him in. We brought him in. His mother let him come in. We picked him up at the train. We had a jam session. The play was wonderful.
Tell me, I'm not trying to embarrass you or anything, but did you ever learn to read any at all much?

No, I never took a lesson. I took one lesson from Jerry Schrimmer. He says, that's Gene Caffarelli's stepfather. He used to run the con company. He says, your ear's too good. He says, you can't learn to read music. You heard by hearsay. I took one lesson. And my brother Henny taught himself how to read. And after he learned how to read, he passed away. Yeah. That's why I was superstitious. I was afraid to learn how to read.
Well, it certainly is.
I've been doing better than a lot of guys that's reading.
I have no complaints. You can play anything. It's remarkable.
I mean, that... I do have a good ear. That's not egotism. That's right. It's just a fact.
That's a God gift. Anybody that's ever heard you say that. Would you advise young kids, if they have a lot of talent, not to bother to read? Just pick it up and use their...

Well, no. I advise them to take... Get the fundamentals of the horn. Learn the fundamentals through music. And then, after they learn the horn, know the notes. They can listen to records. And listen to those ideas and try to improve the ideas. Be original. Don't imitate them. But listen to those. Say you listen to Miff or Lou McGarry or Tea Garden. If you want to be a tea garden, you listen to tea garden records. And then you try to take what Jack's doing and do it a little better. That's what Ted Lewis always told me. He says, Brunus, when you go out on your own, he says, take something that somebody else does and try to do it better. And he says, when you make a mistake, he says, make a good one. He says, and then pull a gag with the audience. You make them laugh and they'll forget all about your mistake. Yeah. He's a great showman.
Great schooling for talking to an audience. Would you credit Ted Lewis with being the inspiration for your showmanship? That's right. Because everybody knows.
Well, I don't say my showmanship, but to speaking to an audience.
Some of that is boring. I mean, you can't learn.
The rhythm I got in my body. God gave me that.
Yeah. But I mean, just the fact that you got up and cracked these jokes and keep the audience entertained, even in the interaction. Well, they say it's boring.

Bud Friedman used to say, what are you trying to prove? Now Bud's dancing around and telling jokes. And he's singing, I hear. I don't know. I don't know. There was a little professional jealousy in a lot of boys. Every time I worked with them, I don't know what it was. I don't know whether maybe I was gifted a little more on the ball. And then we had a couple of big name bands who used to come in and Nick said, what are you guys trying to prove with that Dixieland two beat stuff? I says, to me, Dixieland ain't strictly two beat. I says, Dixieland is a melody, variations, kind of melody, and a beat. Whether it's two beat or four beat, it's Dixieland. That's a wonderful definition. So this guy's a big man today. And I think I'll mention his name.
That's all you don't have to use if you don't want to do anything you have to.

Well, he's a big man. He sells a lot of records. And he's doing all big band arrangements of the Dixieland numbers that we played. He asked us what we were trying to prove at Nick's. And he's a big man today. Of course, I don't want any suits coming in. I don't like to get up and go to court. I like to get the money if I whip them. So, uh...
Well, how did you learn to play so wonderfully? I mean, you not only have a wonderful ear and wonderful tone, but even your position. I mean, you got around...

Well, Pansy Lane, that's Papa Lane's son. His name is Alfred. They called him Pansy. He played the trumpet and his brother-in-law, Leon Smello. I was playing the upright alto and he was playing the trombone. So he got under the weather one time and he didn't show up. And, uh, we were playing down at Crescent City Carnival Club. And, uh, Pansy says, uh, geez, what are we going to do for a trombone? He says, I said, well, I can play the trombone parts on the alto. He says, why don't you try the trombone, Bruno? So that's when that song was out, How Dry I Am, Now I Am. So I put the trombone again and I started blowing and I liked it. Slide. And then I was thinking all the time of my brother Henny, you know, I said, oh, I could never be that way. So we played and I played that. I did a lot of guesswork, you know, it was new to me. So from that time on, I liked trombone. I threw the alto. The alto was what, uh, what's his name, was playing with Bobby Hackett today, uh, Kerry. That's the horn I used to play for the Mardi Gras parade.
Now, Monk Hazel still uses a...
Well, that's a French horn. Yeah, he uses the ground. Well, it's an alto, but it's a French alto, a mellophone.
Um, did you watch your brother? Is that where you got a lot of ideas?
No, I used to drew when that guy played. I wanted to throw that trombone in the hat rack.
But there never was anybody that actually showed you where the seven positions were? Nothing.
That came, that came natural.
Did you even think about whether you're going in the fourth position or the third or anything? I feel it. You don't even think about that position?
My heart puts my arm there.
Yeah.
Where to put a smear, where to put the right notes. Yeah. It's all done by ear and heart.
Uh, did you ever ask anybody about, uh, advice on tonguing or breathing or anything? No, it came natural.

There's only one man, to me, we never got along. God bless him, he's passed away. To me, he was a great trombonist. And he had something that not even my brother or anybody had. It's what musician termed as a breathing control. And not, he's about the only one I ever heard that controlled it. I heard him at the Paramount one time in New York City. And he played this trombonology. Who was that?
Tommy Dorsey.
Oh, Tommy Dorsey.
Jimmy, I loved.

Jimmy was a sweetheart. I loved it. There was a little jealousy on Tommy and I side, I guess it was. And he played seven choruses on a trombone, with variations and all that tongue and everything. And he hit a high cadenza on the finish with a high F without breathing, taking a breath. Well, I do one thing now and the same. Do-do-do-do-do-do-do-do. But I can only do it for one chorus. Yeah, that's good. But he, oh, this, this, this man was fabulous for breathing control. Uh, but Jimmy was a doll. I mean, I love Jimmy.
Did, uh, did you ever actually practice by yourself, get the thing and try to learn? Never warm up. Never warm up.

That's what Peewee and Davis and all them guys, they'd be down at Nick's, they'd be warming up in the back for 15 minutes. I'd walk right off the street and go one, two, right into the number and they'd say,
how does this guy do it? He's got an iron lip.
Yeah, I agree. And they'd warm up there for two, three, 15 minutes and they'd come out and they'd crack all over the place.
You never tried practicing long notes?
Never, never for tone or nothing. Nothing. Just natural. It was God gifted.

Yeah, that's right. It must be. You didn't. Still, you must have worked on it. I mean you played so many jobs. Oh yeah. Tell me about, can you remember any, the first parade you played or any other parades?
Oh man, that's, I was six years old. How big were you?
Really?

I used to play snare drums sometimes with Tony Spago at the Dixieland Band and Biloxi in the Crockett Parade. He'd say, Bruno, take my drums, I'm tired. He's playing with, he's with the original New Orleans Dixieland Jazz Band. He plays the kazoo.
Yeah, still in New York I guess, yeah.
Tony's a good drummer.
The first parades then you probably played alto horn.
Yeah, alto, and when the drummer didn't show up I had to switch the drums.

Oh, another question when you were speaking of Papa Lane, the Suburban Park. Papa Lane, we had an interview with him last year before our Ford Foundation grant went through. And he mentioned Suburban Park, was it? In McDonaville.

Or across the river. You see there's Gretna, there's McDonaville, and there's Algiers. Then up the upper part is Harvey's and West Wego and it's on the other side of the river. And the Crescent City Park is in Gretna, there's Bourbon Park, there's in McDonaville, and the Elvira Park is in Algiers. Then there was a club right on the river there by the ferry boat called the Owls Club, we used to play there a lot.
Well you have a cousin over there, I've never met him, I've been in the place, runs a little corner saloon. Oh, Whitey's?
Yeah, that's it. Yeah, he plays trombone good.
He plays with the jukebox. Yeah, that's right.
He plays better trombone than a lot of guys I know up here, and he just taught himself with the jukebox.
Yeah, we're going to over and interview him some of these days.
Oh, I tell you, he looks something like Darcy, but he's much bigger, and he's always a bruiser.
Is he younger than you, or about your age?
Oh yeah, he's a lot younger than me. I don't know about how many years, but he's a wonderful guy. He's got a crazy saloon over there.
Yeah, I've been in there once, but I didn't know who, several years ago, I didn't know who ran it.
He surprised me when he sat down and put them jukebox nickels in and started playing.
Yeah, the first time I heard that, I thought there was a band in there playing. I ran in there to see, and there he was playing.
Well, he idolizes me. He thinks there's nobody in the world like me.
Yeah, I don't blame him.

He dropped everything. Monte Gros Day, I walked in there. Dixie and I walked in there. He says, my Uncle George is here. Drop everything. And he had it loaded with these- Oh, he's your nephew then? Yeah, my sister's boy. Abou would have dropped dead. That's my cousin. That's my- Yeah, that's my-

Oh, they tell me too, every once in a while you hear stories about, like you say, you fellows didn't, you all turned out well and all that. But they say that they used to play a lot of tricks and there's something Raymond Burketh started to tell us once about a coffin or something you all fixed up. Maybe, or was that your older brother's? I never asked him about that. A coffin? Yeah, like an undertaker's part of it.
Oh, my brother. Have we played a joke?
Some silly joke or crazy practical joke we did. Do you remember anything about that?

Oh, an undertaker. We used to hang around the undertakers and play cards in the afternoon. Ernie was a part-clown player and he was an embalmer. So we used to sit around and Uncle Fritz was the undertaker. He looked just like Matt Berman. We used to sit around and kid around. So his cousin, Brother Lites, they'd go to the Orpheum scene, take their wives, and then if there's anything happening, they'd page him and tell him there was a body in the morgue to embalm and fix him up. So my crazy brother, Abbie, there was a little trouble down there with Italians and he'd talk in his face with Nelson's cocoa and he laid on it- We laid him on a table with a sheet over him, you know, and put the basket there and the dim light and the embalming tools. So Uncle Fritz called up the Orpheum and paged Ernie and says, look, Ernie, there's a body in the morgue. He says, fix him up. So we're in the back, you know, you can see right in the morgue room. We're sitting under the hearse and we're laughing like hell. So they lived upstairs. The undertaker lived upstairs. So Brother Lites would go in the office to make out the death notice for the paper and Ernie would walk in the back, take his coat off, roll up his sleeve and put a hunk of chew tobacco in his mouth. So, this dim light is on and he pulls out and he chews the back and lifts up the sheet and my brother goes, ah! The guy run, chew tobacco, swallow tobacco and Ernie Hintz got on the steps and he hollered, oh ma, oh ma, he couldn't move, he was so stuck. We died laughing at that. We've talked about that for years.
I never heard anything about that.
Only Abbie would think of that.
Yeah, Abbie never told us about that. Raymond Burk had heard it and told me about it once.
And Abbie was crazy. He's a great guy, boy. That guy can build more things. Did you see, were you in Biloxi?
Just one night to hear him.
See the thing he built there, that little diner in that house? He built that on himself.
I didn't see that, no. I saw the place over there they were playing there.
Oh, Barra Seeds. They're back there again.
No, they're a different place now.
No, they're back. Dixie just got a letter from them.
Oh, that, I didn't know.
What's the name's going up for auction next week, Broadwater? Oh, the Broad. Well, the same guy as the manager, Love, Darling. What's his name? Love, I think his name is.
I didn't know.
Well, they're back at Barra Seeds.
We'll get over there pretty soon to see him again.
That's a great town.
Well, the part of town you were raised in, is that actually called the Irish Channel that you were in?

That's one block from the Mississippi River on Chapitula Street. We lived on 2135 Roussau. And two blocks down was what they termed the Irish Channel. They used to give lawn parties there. You know what they call a lawn party down there? Oh, yeah. I've heard about them. They had oyster shells and bricks coming up out of the ground. They'd get a tapu, you know, off the cotton on the river and put it down. People would dance on that. Then they'd hire a band and at 12 o'clock come, they'd say, Well, how about the overtime? He says, It's 12 o'clock. He says, Well, we just sent out for another ballad bass. He says, Keep playing. So they'd keep playing. The guys would beat it off with the money. Wouldn't pay the musicians.
Oh, okay.

They used to shoot cops in the feet and make them dance. Really? They'd throw bricks back. And then the bunch from Basin Street used to come up and call those with brick bats. And I was a signal man. I used to give them this, I'd be the watch out man. When they'd come, I'd go, That means for the guys to get ready, they'd come in there. Brick boarders used to fight like a dick.
Really?

Throwing bricks back. You'd go from Basin Street to pick on the channel. Then the channel would go down to Basin Street. Oh, that was years ago, my God. Were they mostly Irish? See that neighborhood now, you never know it.
You're a French descent, aren't you?
No, German and part of Belgium I think.
Belgium, well that's practically French too, isn't it? I never did know for sure.
My grandfather was born in Lipschick, Germany. And if the Kaiser would have won that war, we'd have been very wealthy people. Which I'm glad he didn't.
Yeah, was their name Brunis or another?
B-R-U-N-I-E-S. That's the German way.
Oh, is that right? I didn't know. Anything else you can remember when you were a kid? Any of the first music you ever heard aside from home? Were there other bands around?
Well, there was a band on a color band called Sweet Buddy Petit. There was, Papa Lane used to call his band the Reliance band. And then we played on a streetcar, Emmet Rogers.
Oh yeah, tell me about that.

And Abby, we had a uniform. Abby had leader, I had manager, and Emmet Rogers on the drums had Brunis on his hat. And we used to play in a sightseeing car. We made good money. We used to point out the interesting points of New Orleans, these three guys. And then we'd play, you know, like harmony and stuff. Then Rogers would go through with the hat, passing the hat through the thing. We made $15, $20 a day.
He'd sit at one end of the car, stand at one end of the car and play there.

So one day we sent Rogers out for coffee and he got all excited and laughed and he happened to... His nose went into the coffee, you know. We wouldn't drink it so that's how we'd give him the name of Snotsy Rogers. Oh yeah. That's what the name of Snotsy Rogers we used to call. That's a good name.
That's a good name. I believe it was something... Boy, if you could only make money in that town, it's fabulous.
Yeah.
Do you remember playing at the French market? Abby said you'd...
We used to put the celery and what's the name, and our lapels. Yeah. Played for the butchers over there.
Go right into the French market, the stalls there?
Well we played like the unemployed bands in England, you know. Yeah.
Play on the corner. Did you take up a collection then too? Have a hat?

Well we didn't do it but they'd hand us money, you know. They figured we were unemployed or poor as them. It was all kicks those days, we didn't care. We didn't figure things would be like the other day.
No.
I wish I knew then I'd be worth a million.
Yeah, you worked it right. Do you remember Fischer's band?

Oh yeah, he was a pretty good client at that time. Fischer and George Schilling played trombone. Well I've talked to Hal Schilling. And there was Diddy Stevens, and there was Darren Hughes, and there was a patch over his eye. We used to play the Advertiser Fights, and walk around the streets and we had a fight on there, and Kit Costner used to play trombone. The night he was fighting he'd come play and watch the street with us, the night before he was going in the fight. He was going in the fight.
He must have been a tough guy.

And they used to stop on the corner in the bar rooms, you know, you'd play a couple of numbers and get you in and have a drink. They used to sit me on the bar and save me booze. That's what stunned my growth. I should be six foot something. Oh I don't know.
That would have made a difference. Yeah they say alcohol stunned your growth. I was young then.
Merritt isn't much taller than you. Merritt isn't much taller than you. No.
I said to Merritt, I said, holy or not Merritt, he says, 62. He says, that's not my age, that's the weather temperature I'd say.

There was a guy come in the club about two weeks ago, his name was Alexandra. He says, your brothers have got a pretty good band. He says, they played for our convention down in Bilox at the Buena Vista. He says, they got a pretty good band for a bunch of guys. He says, but tell me, how does your brother get music out of that patched up trombone he's got? Yeah, it's all patched up with tape. I'm going to buy him one and send him one. He likes it, he's used to it. Did you ever play a valve trombone? Did you ever try a valve trombone? Oh yeah, I can play that. Did you ever play a card? I got a tape, I got a tape, he was used to it.
Did you ever play a valve trombone?
Oh yeah, I can play that. Did you ever play card?
I got a tape, I got a tape that we took last New Year's.
Of course we were all blind at Abby's house, you know. And we were trying to play three way of harmony with the trombone and two trombones or two trumpets and trombone.
They do a lot of that on the job. Yeah, that's what they like.

They specialize in that harmony, that's pretty stuff. Of course it's barbershop, a lot of these progressive guys that call it corn and inky, but that's what started music. To me, blues comes from the Jewish hymn, like Ailey Ailey. Yeah. Then they took the African bongos or tom-tom and they made rhythm to it. That's my opinion of blues. The blues.
Oh, of all.
And to me all blues sound alike.
Well they are somewhat, and they slow blues. Tell me about Ken Roof Blues when you all first played that. Was that worked out up here?
Well, it was Paul and I. We used to call it the Rusty Rail Blues.
Well that's right, I heard the name.
So we came up here, Melrose, Waller Melrose, the publisher, which I gave him the title of the house of blues built for his bottom of his music. He's in the real estate business out in Barrington.
Yeah, I remember seeing that.

He came up and he liked the tune, he gave us $500 advance. He just heard the tune at Fry's. Yeah. So he says, you don't mind if I do anything with it? He's never been to New Orleans. So he says, we're going to change the title to the, that was a place called the Suburban Gardens. We used to call it the Tin Roof Cafe.
Yeah. Where was that?
New Orleans, out in Gentilly. Out towards Gentilly.
Yeah.

And he took it and he put these lyrics to it. I've seen the bright lights burning up and down Broadway, there's no lights burning like my hometown. And, well then at that time we put rap in, no rap Paul and I, and then we put Mel Stitzel and Ben Pollock in, you know, because we didn't figure it was going to do anything.
No, just put all the names down.

So, years later, after 28 years, you suppose a copywriter tune, I didn't figure, I figured it was nothing. Because I was getting $12 and $8 on, you know, the royalties. So one day I hear this thing, take me in your arms and never let me go. I says, man, that's Tin Roof, note for note. So I call up Teenie, that's Captain Harris' sister, that's Paul's wife. So I says, Teenie, have you got the copyright on Tin Roof? She says, yes, and you can thank me because I just had it renewed because those guys had it, copyrighted, and they were going to try to have it copyrighted and they were going to steal it. So I said, man, you saved a day. So she did, she had it copyrighted. After 28 years, you know, if you don't have it copyrighted. Yeah, that's a good thing. You have to split that royalties in many ways, of course. Well, and we got the guy, they played it the other night on the hit parade, this kid put the lyrics to it, this Copeland. He says, one of the writers. Well to me, what sold the song is a melody. Well I think so. You can't get one person that can sing you the melody to the make love to them, but they can sing. I used to hear cops on the street whistling. It's the melody that sold it. So he's in on it, and Melrose got the publishers right, and I got the writer, and Paul, and Pollock, Teenie. So we made a few bucks, it wasn't much, but it was too many split.
Yeah. Is there anything of interest to your trombone soul, how you first, you might say, created that thing, you know, starting on that low note and all?
No, we just played . Then we played . Then rap took that high chorus, and it was printed to me and I played . Just played what felt natural.
Came into your head. Because everybody copies that, mostly note for note.
Windy won high trombone play, he says, can you play Brunus' chorus on tin roof? He says, if you can you get the job. He's got a kid from Mexico, he calls him the Brunus of Tijuana, Jack somebody.
Oh, he was up here once. Jack Flores? Yeah, sure, he was here at the 11-11 one time on a Sunday, I remember. And Wingy came through.
He calls him the Brunus of Tijuana.
Yeah, that's probably the most copied and most famous trombone song.
You know, Wingy, you know that thing that the late Glenn Miller made, In a Mood? Yeah. That was Wingy's tune.
That's right, it's the riff.
He had the proof that he wrote, he had a record of Tall Paper Stomp, he called it.
Yeah, I remember.

And he got a lot of money out of that from Glenn Miller. He didn't. Wingy's a pretty shrewd boy when it comes to money. Yeah. He acts illiterate but he's pretty smart. He's like Maxie Rosenblum. Yeah. Musical Maxie Rosenblum.
Oh, I was going to ask if you could tell a little bit about rap, because he's not here to speak for himself anymore.
Him and Fazola to me were the men.
What kind of a clarinet did he play? I guess Albert's system, do you remember? I don't remember.
I think it was, no, I think it was Baum's system.
You don't remember any details, like what kind of reeds he used? No.
I never heard about his instrument, you know, because I didn't know anything about the clarinet.
Did he ever practice much, or was he pretty much natural?
Oh, he used to run over variations a little bit, you know. And the only one the band could read was Elmer Filmer. One night we surprised Mike Fritz, and we knocked off the Song of Indy.
He says, man, you guys play that thing like it wasn't written, or should I? I said, we sure do.
He says, but it's good. Hey, it was a great cafe man, boy. He did more for jazz guys in those days than a lot of people today. People don't realize it.
I'm sorry we didn't get to talk to him. We would have interviewed him. Oh. He died now.
You should ask my brother Merritt about him. He'll know. He loved Merritt.
He'll know. He can tell us something about him. I'll see if there's any more questions about the early days I can ask you. Did you play at Millenburg?

Oh, yeah. We used to go out there on weekends, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. Everybody had a camp, you know. You'd walk out about a block on water. One time I'm playing out there, and I'm full Italian boy. And the water's only up to here, you know, around the camp. So I'm playing, I make a shmear, but then the slide goes off and it falls down the lake. So I got to, we were playing the bathing suits. I had to go down and look around the lake for my slide. Oh, I was pitched out full of wine. But they'd go on for weekends. They'd have a colored band here and a white band here and a colored band there. They'd all be blowing against each other. That's why they called it the Millenburg Jaws. Down there they say Millenburg Jaws.
They'd say Millenburg. I don't know how that started up here, but down there in Millenburg. Did you ever play at Bucktown any time?
Oh yeah, that's how I got in the union.
Where was it?
It was a place called Bruning's and Martin's.
I think Martin's is still there, huh?

Well, my uncle owned that last. He sold it out before he died. He bought Martin out and it was called Brunus and Bruning's. No relations. Yeah. So Bruning wanted me. I sat in there one time and I was in the union. I was a punk kid. So Bruning's is, the drummer at Bruning's was the secretary of the union. He says, I want this boy in the union. He says, I want him to work here. So he put up the $50 and I went, I had to go down to the union for examination, you know. Yeah. So I went in on cymbals. What was that? To get in the union. So they put up the piano player when he tries out, he played, the number I know by backwards, they goes to the spirits of independence. I started doing it. He says, you're in, that's enough.
You got in as a cymbal player.
I couldn't get into reading a trombone.
Yeah, they'd make you read something.
They thought I was reading it.
Yeah. That's what I mean. For the trombone, they would have put up something.
That's what the drummer told me. He says, take the cymbals, it's easy.
Yeah.
So I made the introduction. Boom, boom, boom. Ching, boom, boom. Crazy.
How old were you then about when you got in the U?
Oh, about 16 or 17.
Oh, is there any more you can tell about that one picture we had here, Papa Lane's band?
Oh.
Oh, do you remember, are they calling, as you say, some people call him Pansy Lane, the name he didn't like?
Well, we went as imposters. We got a job in Alexander, Louisiana.
Yeah.

We posed as the original Dixieland jazz band. And they had a beautiful Victrola on the Battle House Hotel on the porch. And these soldiers, you know, sit on the lawn and these people are guests. And they played the liver stable blues. And we learned it just note for note. Like, so one guy in the audience is a soldier. He says, look, I know the Dixieland band. Those guys are imposters. So the mayor made us get out of town.
Oh, really? Yeah.
So I was broke. I'm always broke on them jobs. So I didn't want to send home for money. It was only Alexander, Louisiana. Ain't far from New Orleans.
No.

So I went to work in a restaurant. I didn't know anybody or anything. So I had to work 16 hours a day. So to work in a restaurant, I had a needle shot in my arm. The government kind of the soldiers. So this crazy noise breaks a needle off my arm. My arm swells up. So it finally got wet and I went in there. And that's where I learned how to haul a bowl of chili, a bowl of hell, and an oyster stew, a cemetery special. I learned all the waitresses things. I was getting $16 a week and all I could eat in 16 hours a day work. So I didn't stay there. I got enough fare to go back to New Orleans. Then there was a play there in this place where we had this picture taken. I got the Air Dome. Had this stock company. And I played a Jap valet. All I had to do was be made up like a Jap and walk in and say, dinner is served, dinner is served. That was my line. I got paid so much a night for that.
For being an actor too. This personnel is right the way it's given here in the second line, Charlie Cardella.
Yeah, he was very good. He played with Abbott at the halfway house.
Yeah, I know. Some record kind of it. Jules Reiner, piano. Do you know anything about him? No. I don't know that name.
No. I know the bass player, but I can't think of his name.
It says here Herman Ragus. Is that any relation to the piano player?
Henry Ragus.
Henry was a piano player at the original Dixieland Shields.
That could have been Ragus.
It says Herman.
Let me see. That might be Ragus.
Would it be the same fella, Henry? Or was there a brother, maybe Herman?
No, that looks like Henry Ragus. I think that's before he went up with the Dixieland.
Yeah, it might be. No, let's see, 1919. No, they...
Well, that's when he left the Dixieland. Then they got Willard Robinson, or Russell... No, Conrad. Con Conrad played the piano with him.
Yeah, I thought he died there.
This Ragus left the Dixieland, came back to New Orleans or something.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well, do you know how Pansy Lane got that name? Pansy Lane got that name. I think Raymond says he was called Pansy.
No, Julius Reiner is the piano, and Herman Ragus is the bass player.
Yeah, that's what I wondered about the bass player.
No, that's a different...
Is it your mother of the same family, or...?
Might be. But Reiner is the piano player.
Yeah.
Give it a haircut on me there, will you?
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, that was some days, boy.
Well, this hasn't much bearing, really, on our story, but I've wondered how late was your father living? When did he die, about?
When did he die? I don't remember.
Before your mother, or...?
Oh, yeah, he died before my mother.
Before when your mother died, when you were just joining... That's...
Yeah. When did my father die? 19... I had to have someone.
Did he play professionally, or did he have another job, or what did he do? Who? Your father.

My father was the hotel... Hotel... The... Of all the Mexican Gulf hotels. He made up all the menus. Oh, was that right? He did the buying. He had a pretty good job. Mm-hmm. And all his menus, all his recipes were used in all the Mexican Gulf hotels in the Southern Territory. Right. He supervised them. He was a hell of a baker. Ooh, brother. What a baker that man was.
Do you remember much about...
That's why we all learned how to cook. Richie was a good cook. I cook fairly well. Abby's a wonderful cook. My sister, my other brother Richie, was working on the coil boats.
That's right, I heard that.
He was cooking for the crew, and they went crazy for his food.
Yeah.
Richie's in a bad way now.
I'm sorry to hear that. I was going to ask, do you remember anything about the old district in New Orleans? Did you ever play up there?
Well, I played through there during the fight. You know, we'd go out and march through there. When they closed...
Yeah.
When Matt Berman closed the district.
Yeah, when it closed in the war.
Well, I went through there playing New York, my God of the... And funeral marches.
You were there then?

Yeah. And I went back there one night, and my mother beat the diggers at me. I used a pair of long pants, and that's what I said. That was when I started posing as a midget, you know, putting black marks on my hair, and my head looked like wrinkles. And the cop thought I was a schoolboy, and he said, he's a midget. And I used to make my voice look like an old man.
Pretty good. You remember much about Mardi Gras time. Anything special, parades then?

Well... Most of the time, the people down there did high crazy things like carriages and horses and things, and they'd all get a group. They'd all go in groups, and then everybody has open house. You either have a drink, or you have donuts and chocolate, or... They're supposed to serve you something. It's traditional. And then they had the segregation on it. The colored people used to wear certain masks, so if they could tell who it was.
Well, they did like that.

Yeah. And the... What was it? The nightclubs would be open all day, and they'd pass the frying pans around. All day long, there's music going on in the cabarets and everything. I mean, that's when the musicians used to look forward to that day. That's when they made a lot.
Yeah.
10, 12 times a day, they'd pass this frying pan around. Everybody was drunk.
Did you do much marching on Mardi Gras and some of the carnival clubs? Oh, yeah.
Sometimes I'd play for the garden districts or different clubs. Oh, yeah. Sometimes I'd play for the garden districts or different clubs.

Oh yeah, sometimes I'd play for the Garden Districts or different clubs and most of the time I'd play for Pop Lane and there was a guy named Mars hired all the bands. They used to hire my brother Richie two years in advance because he was the only guy with a little cornet that could hold a 17 piece brass band and put one cornet. They'd stop at City Hall and hear Richie coming. There comes Richie Bruns. They could tell him. Every course would go up an octave higher or a key higher. I see one day his lip was bleeding dripping all over me.
He's still playing now.
Boy, he had an iron lip.

In those days did the Rex, nowadays the Rex parade will use a lot of high school bands, American Legion, Boy Scouts, Buccal Corps. In those days did they use some... Now it's gone. We were talking about Mardi Gras, the bands playing.

Yeah, the union was more stronger than there's more non-union musicians on the non-air union. There's no union at all in Biloxi. Yeah, that's right. Because they didn't want union and the non-union guys would make more than the union men. And the people in Biloxi didn't want the union.
Now those brass bands on Mardi Gras, how big a band would that be?
Well they'd have two tubas, two baritos, two altos, two trombones, about four clarinets, four or five trumpets.
Pretty big bands. Yeah. Twenty-five pieces maybe or so.

And then they'd have the drum corps and the police band or something. Now they're putting high schools and all of them. Of course they'd get paid. We used to get seven parades. We'd get thirty-five dollars when I was playing them. We'd play one on a Thursday and then the following Monday we'd have to play a Monday day parade and a Monday night and then the Tuesday day parade and a Tuesday night parade. It was five parades. We got seven dollars an hour. I mean seven dollars a parade.
A parade, yeah. How much did the dancers pay in those days when you played, say, out at Millenburg? Those were called picnics.
We used to get fifty cents an hour.
Fifty cents an hour. I was going to ask a little bit more about your trombone. If you like a big bell or a little bell better, if there's any difference?
Well, the one I'm so used to now, that's a medium bore.
Yeah, about medium bore.

It all depends on the person himself. If they study it, they have to get used to something. The advice is to get used to the horn first before you start taking lessons, that you're able to blow it properly. But the bore, some people like small bore for high notes. I specialize in low notes, bass notes. Yeah.
What kind of mouthpiece do you use?
I got an H-N-Y, A-Q-E, A-Q-E, A-Q-E, or something like that. It's 28.
I know people, like you say, it's not good for some kid to just try to imitate you exactly.
Well, I mean, it wouldn't be good for a kid to go out and buy a 28. Maybe a different size would make a different sound for him.
Still, some people are going to be interested in knowing just what kind of mouthpiece you use.
I used to see in those books, buy a Benny Goodman mouthpiece and play like Benny Goodman. So asinine.
Yeah. But some people would wonder just what's going on.

I know Nick LaRocca's brother with the Dixieland band, his brother, tried to learn trauma, and he played and tried and tried. He could hardly get a note out of it. He tried, he threw it against the wall, he got mad. It wasn't in him. It's got to be in you. I don't know. If you haven't got it, you haven't got it.
Have you had any advice on the style? What kind of a part to play? That is, some people call that the vamp style, sort of like a bass style?

No, the nucleus of Dixieland is a good lead trumpet, unless he's playing a solo. Variations on the clarinet, and the contra melody they call on the trombone. That's the contra melody. Then the piano plays a good umpire chord, because Dixieland bands in those days never used a bass fiddle. They only had five pieces. And the drummer, he can play four, he can play two, any way he feels, you know, all the way. Like when we're playing over here, and the apple will say, give me two. So hey, hey, give him two beats. And when I'm playing ensemble, I holler, walk it. And he knows what I want. That's what I call home cooking. That's cymbal, four on here and on his cymbal. So that's march tempo. Four beats with the pedal. Yeah, that's what I call him. I holler, walk it. And he knows what I want. I call it home cooking.
Is there anything you have, the suggestions on the tempo, whether you play faster or slower on some of these things?
Well, some place you go, some people like slow music. Some place you go there, they don't want to hear slow music. They like the fast music.
I notice in general, some of the New Orleans fellas, they usually stick to a slower tempo, whereas some of the more modern guys have had to rush everything.
Well, Muggy's got a tendency to play a lot of fast music.
Yeah, that's right.

And over here, we open state with a number like Musgrad or Jasmine Blues. And then the second number we'll either play Jatter or, what's that thing, Someday Sweetheart or Squeeze Me. And then we'll build a semi-fast number like Strutters Ball or Georgia Brown. And we close with the Rampart or something bright again. Give them a little different variety.
But I meant to say, take a piece like, well, Saints Go Marching In. I just played the band.
Well, you can play that fast.
Sometimes I play that so fast you could never march to it. That's right. But more of the real New Orleans bands I find.
You've got, like Panama and that stuff, those are march tunes. You've got to play march tempo. You can't play a racehorse tempo with this kind of tone.
Yeah, that's what I wanted to know.
You don't feel it if the beat ain't there. We call it circus music.
Yeah. Some people talk about that circus style that the Dixieland trombonists use with a lot of slides and all that.

Well, I tell you, I listened to an old guy, Ricky Toms, who's a great circus man. He was a terrific executioner. That's the first time I ever saw him use cut a cure salve and water on a slide. What? Cut a cure salve and water to make the horn slide. I use cold cream. Now, it's the same thing.
You use cold cream on there. What is this when you squirt though?
That's water. Water. Oh. Water and cold cream makes it slippery.
But you rub cold cream on the slide?
Yeah, and then wipe the slide off and then squirt the water and then put a little more cold cream and then you get a slippery slide.
No, I didn't know. I thought it was an oil you were squirtin'.

No, it makes an oil you like the greasy street. If it rains, it gets slippery. Sure. Yeah. So I couldn't stand that other Holt and Trombone oil they had. It was citronella and you used to inhale that stuff and get in your lungs. I mean your stomach. You know, when you breathe that, bring that horn in and there's a suction that goes down your throat, it brings air up. And you inhale it every time you breathe in. So cold cream is clean and it smells nice.
Yeah, I never thought. Sure. That's a good suggestion. Anything about the care of the instrument or anything you do?
No, just keep it clean. The tea garden cleans these out after every set. I clean mine out every month.
And yet it's lasted 47 years.

I had it fixed twice, I think, I sent it in. I said, I'm sorry, I'm used to that horn. I don't even have it insured. I did lose it once and I was sober as a judge in New York. I took this, he was a racketeer and he was drunk and I wanted to take care of him so he wouldn't get in no trouble. So we got down to Mulberry Street and I got my horn. I got to play for Blesch that day, you know, this is jazz. So I leave the trombone in the cab and we get out at the Patsy's to get pizza and stuffed artichokes. Man, I went crazy. I lost that horn. I looked around six, seven days. I called every police station in New York and finally, way down, way down town, way, way down. Guy found it for me, a sergeant. He says, come on down and get it and see if you can identify it. So I identified, it was mine.
Yeah, I was lucky, I guess. Gee.
Boy, I've lost it man. I go crazy. I'm so used to it.
Yeah. They still make the Kings, I guess, but not that model probably.
Well, I don't know. They put inferior material in horns today.
Does it seem a little heavier than some of them or?
No, I don't like a balance or any heavier. I like a horn where I can throw it. See? Yeah. Them balances put you back and keep your head up. And I like to play down, up, and this way, and that way.

Yeah, that's right. I notice you do get around all of it. And Henry did all those stunts too, you say. Then like, oh, you had this one stunt. I never remember seeing you do it lying on the floor and people standing on your stomach.
No, Henry didn't do that one. That was a dare. I seen a, believe it or not, once at Nick's.
Yeah.

Read the paper and I saw this guy standing on his head smoking a cigarette playing the trombone. So I said, I think I'll go with one better. So I took two chairs and put my heels there on my neck. Let the guy stand on him, hold one foot and play the trombone with my foot while the guy stand on my stomach. Yeah, I never saw that. It was in Time Magazine. They took it down and hit the brass reel.
I never even saw that. Any other stunts that Henry did? I remember seeing a picture of him sitting up on a piano or something playing too, I believe.
Yeah, he played on a piano. He used to jump.
No, I mean sitting on top of playing his trombone or something up on the piano.

Oh, well, that's traditional in New Orleans. Most of a lot of guys sat on top of the piano. But he had a habit of shimmying. He'd sing and I'm ready for a break. He'd jump off the stand and shimmy and then jump back on the stand and start playing again. He did that in Blux one night and he liked the chief of police's daughter. The chief of police didn't like him so he put him in jail.
Oh, jeez. Poor guy.
He was fabulous on that horn, boy. Holy God.
How was his tone? Well, he made a couple of records. The first time I heard him on the record I thought it was you.
Wonderful boy.
So it was very similar to your tone.
To me, I think the greatest tone I ever heard on the trombone was Jerry Shimmer. Played with Susie, he was a teacher.
Jerry Shimmer?
Shimmer. He always, I got a picture of him there somewhere. He was about 80-some-odd. He was supposed to come down and see me.
Still living?

Yeah, he stood in the next room the day I went to take a lesson. He was playing a, I forget the name of the tune, but it sounded like a human voice. The most beautiful thing I ever heard on the trombone of my life. And to me, the best record today for trombone, the way I think trombone should be played and sounded, is this Murray McAckred. Oh, yeah. He made a record of Sleepy Time Girl with the Casaloma Band. After that you can take the record. But he plays that so beautiful and phrases so wonderful. And for trumpet, there's Bobby with Funny Valentine and I like that stuff.
What's your favorite record that you made yourself, if you had to pick one or two?
I don't know. They all seemed the same to me.
Of course, the old New Orleans rhythm kings, you've never, nobody surpassed that tin roof blues.
Well, the record was supposed to be my record date to get Davis' name on it. That's a plenty, it's a 12-inch.
Oh, yeah, that one, yeah, that's a good one.

That was supposed to be my record date. So, Mill Gables says, look, you've got your name on record. He says, Davis is going in the army, let's put his name on the push. And I says, alright, it's supposed to be my date.

Yeah, that's funny, I remember that. That would be one I would pick too, is one of your outstanding. And then the old tin roof blues that you did for your net. Anything about that date you can tell about those first records you made?

Well, first day I got in there, I think the bugle car was the first thing we made, and I started blasting on that horn, boy, and the records start jumping all around. So they made me turn around, play to the wall, and get the blast from the wall into the horn.
Oh, really?
And then an argument came up with Jelly Roll and Paul Merez were going to record this, I don't know what it was, Malenburg or one of those two.
They did London blues, maybe?
Well, I wanted to do Don't Get Funky on the Water. And I'll call it my brother Bill going across the field, what do you call it? Louie made a record of it.
Oh yeah, Brother Bill or something.
So, uh...
What was the title you called it down there?
Don't Get Funky on the Water. Don't Get Funky on the Water.
Yeah, on the water.

On the water. You know, it goes swimming and fishing and... Yeah. So, uh, an argument coming, I walked out of the studio, I didn't want to play it. I didn't want to play the other thing, I wanted this tune, I wanted to hear it on wax. So then Paul come out and talked me into it and cursed me and said, and I went back and saw it.
Was Jelly rolled on that first date, do you remember? Or was it...?

No, I don't think so. I think he went on a second date. I think, uh... Mel Stitzel. Or Elmas Show, but I think it was. I can't quite remember. Yeah, I know. It's a long time. 40 years, isn't it? Soon will be. 36 years ago, I guess.

Since they made those things. You've made those down in Richmond, Indiana. Yeah. How long did you stay on that trip? Is that a day or two? Two or three days, I think. It took Ted Lewis with Jimmy Dorsi on the clarinet to make Ann Hague's children blues. We made it from 10 o'clock in the morning, 6 o'clock in the night, and we just finished it.

Really? Oh, yeah. Every time we'd get going good, something would happen. Yeah. Vandu would pop a string, or somebody would talk, or forget or say something, we'd have to keep making it over. Yeah. That was a fabulous guy, that Lewis. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. with Chauncey Morehouse, Charlie Spivak, Jimmy Lytell, Claude Thornhill, who made them on the Varsity record.
