That's when Spivak says, you know about the blues, teach me how to play a chord. He played a nice chorus of blues on there. I didn't show him nothing. I said, man, just play natural. Nobody can show you that stuff, it has to come to you. Played a nice chorus on it.
Does your lip ever get tired when you play? Do you, some people say the more they play, the better it gets.

Well, right now I got this thing, I point my lip, I've been suffering the last four nights, pressing that mouthpiece up against you. I point it with a cigarette, and I hope it'll be all right tonight.
Ordinarily though, you would never tire in a night, would you?

Well, Billy Roush and I, he's a very good trauma player, played Smoke Rins with Casalama. We had a three hour talk one night, he says, you see these guys running around with drugstores and their cases, and they put this on their lip? He says, if you keep yourself moving, he says, Cleen, he says, you'll never have lip trouble, he says. But your stomach is upset, he says, you'll never have trouble. He says, if your stomach upset, you'll start getting fever, cold sores and things. Then these guys put the camphorfenic and all that stuff on there. I just press them and break them, that's all, and blow it to them.
Do you use much pressure, or are you conscious of pressing? It all depends.

Sometimes I use a lower lip, a butt's name lip. I have this here, see? And sometimes, when I got this thing, I'll put them on a piece way up here and use this, one quarter and this one three quarters. Three quarters on the upper lip. But when my lip is good, I use this one quarter and this one three quarters. One quarter on the upper and three quarters on the upper.
And then hold the horn up.
Yeah, hold the horn up higher.
Do you change around then sometimes? Yeah.
When you're a... Well, I've got what they call a freak lip, like Louie, they say.
Yeah.

Louie's got it. Louie does things with little scabs and things on the lip. He can do it. That's what you call born natural, the natural freak lip. Muggsy calls me iron lip. Yeah. I'm a little bit crazy. I'm a little bit crazy. Ha, ha, ha.
Is there anything else you'd like to tell about your early New Orleans days, either playing with your family bands or the first dance jobs you played, who else was in the band?

Oh, I can't remember them now. So many fellows you've played. Papaline had a special band. We played a dance one night. It was cornet, Nicola Rocca, Martin Kirsch on clarinet, me on upright alto and drums. And we played the Lucky One dance hall up in Harvey and there were so many people in there, the thing fell in, the hall fell in.
Or the roof?

Yeah, well the dance floor. Or the dance floor fell in. It was on the second floor and it crashed in. Oh gee, anybody hurt? Yeah, not killed but they were hurt. And he'd send that band around. It was four pieces. No piano. The bands down there were cornet, clarinet, trombone, upright alto, baritone, tuba and drums. We never used the first, the only time we used pianos was when they were in the nightclubs. We were on these picnics and dancing things, they used the brass band.
Yeah. Do you remember some of the other trombone players like Tom Brown, for instance? I'll turn it off. You were talking about the dance bands, Papaline had several bands.

Well, yeah, he was the, years ago they used to have a bookie here. I used to book all the bands. He was the, I can't think of his name now. And he had this one favorite band. If they wanted a four piece band, he'd send this Martin Kirsch, myself on Up Right Al Tua, Nick LaRocca, and himself on drums. That was supposed to be a dance band. Yeah, they couldn't afford no more.
Yeah. I started to ask you, did you know Tom Brown, got to hear him when you were young?
Yeah, they were terrific. They came up here. That's when Shields and Yellow Nunes switched jobs.
Yeah.
Yellow Nunes came up with the original band, and they played on the Red Lantern. A guy by the name of Harry James brought them up here, not the trumpet players. Yes, yeah.
He's still living, I think, in the audience. Yeah.
And then the Brown brothers came up with the farmer's uniforms and the straw hats, and they played. So Yellow Nunes went with the Brown brothers, and Shields went with the Dixieland.
Were they dressed like farmers? No, I didn't know that. I don't think Tom ever told me that.
And his duster's overalls are on, the straw hats.
I have seen a picture like that.
Sun hats.
Supposed to look like farmers.
Yeah.
I didn't know. I don't think Tom ever told me that. Now he's gone.
We talked about it. He's, that's what they said. This guy Murray said he was colored. He wasn't colored.
No, of course not.
That's Steve's brother. And there was another, there was Steve, Tom, there was another one. I don't think he played anything. He was a tin smith. They were all tin smiths.
Oh yeah. They even made violins and basses out of tin. Steve told me about it.
And there's another lawyer counter that used to drive a beer wagon. And he was a tuba player. Bud Lycan.
Oh yeah, Bud.
I think he's...
He died. No, I think he's in a mental hospital now. One of them is.
Then there was Jack Lycan who played left hand trombone.
I didn't know. It was Joe who still plays bass and Arnold is still around. They're the only ones I've met.
That's my, isn't that a foreign magazine?

Yeah, this is that English magazine. I was just checking through here to see if there's any other ideas about your life, any questions here. How did you enjoy working with Joe Merez's brother? I started to say Joe Merez. I'll change this. Paul's. Paul Merez.
He played wonderful. He played wonderful.
I got to hear him and meet him of course too. Is there any advice in playing together that is in harmonies or things that you work on, trumpet and trombone?

Paul is like Muggsy. You have what you call a good drive. And if the trumpet is driving, it makes you drive. That's what I feel. Of course I drive too. If I play with Bobby Haggard, Bobby plays a different style together. To me they all got different styles. You hear Winger, you hear Muggsy, you hear Butterfield, you hear Yank Lawson. They all got different styles.
Do you sometimes consciously try to play sort of a bass part since you don't usually use a string bass in your band or tuba?
That's why I don't want to use a bass because it would interfere with me.
Would interfere with that?
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Larry Shields. Wonderful. His brother plays good too down the road. This person was just here. They think that there's nobody like the Shields playing on it now with Chalky. Yeah, Harry is. She said she never liked Clarence, but she liked him.
Yeah, very good. Any other trombone players? How did Happy Schilling play? He's retired now. I talked to him.

Well, he played mostly valve trombone. Mostly valve, huh. And uh, Esteudian Lane played pretty good. He died. And uh, well as a guy on the coast I liked, Joe Uckel and Abe Lincoln. Oh yeah. Yeah. But Abe tries to do the impossible. He plays high trumpet trombone. Yeah, he's up there awfully high. Yeah. Trombone isn't made for that.
Do you think you're apt to ruin your lip by trying to play too high, or what would you?

Well, you see Teagarden plays nothing but soft solos. And he don't, he don't enforce himself on ensemble. Sometimes you don't know Jack's in the band when they play an ensemble. That's right. Because he saves that lip. His lip is flexible for those pretty little uh, lip trails, the thing he does on the solos. It's what you call a specialist. But if he blasts like I did, he couldn't play them soft solos like he does. He doesn't have. He doesn't have to play one way or the other. Me, I smear into it and I jump up in the microphone and make it.

Yeah. You might use a lot of variety, but you, in the old days, that's what I wonder. I never heard you see 30 years ago. Uh, now you play something so soft and sweet and all to you and then you get the same music.

That's what you call uh, that's what you call shading. Now all the bands are going around there. Like I play in South Rampart Street and I'll say Subdued and then we play soft and then all of a sudden I'll holler walk and then we build it up and we blast and then we're walking down the street.
In the old days did they- It's a contrast. Did they blast more or did you use that contrast?
They just played blah all the way through, blah.
Mostly in the old days.
Yeah.
And you did too little thing when you started out as a kid and that's right.
I just learned that in the last 10 years.
Yeah. What about Henry? Did he have a big range too?
He could play anyway. Anyway.
I imagine he must have.
Anyway, I wish I had a record of him and Emmett Hardy. I only got a record of Emmett Hardy on Trump.
Oh, tell me a little bit about Emmett Hardy. Yeah.

Well, the kid was young. He had leakage of the heart. And if you ask Louie about him, Louie, Louie's a changed man now. All his opinions have changed. Sometime, yeah. And he said that Emmett Hardy was the best.
That's when- You played with them at Little Linn too?
Yeah. On the boat? Yeah, down there. But we never had luck enough to get him on the record.
Yeah, it's too bad. It's a shame.
Bix liked him.
Did his style sound somewhat like Bix, do you think? Some people have said that.
Yeah. Well, I think the closest thing to Bix today is Jimmie McPartland and Red Nichols.
Yeah. But did Emmett Hardy have that same kind of a style or was he more like the other, say, more like-
No, he didn't blast much. He just played little variations and stuff around him, improvised.
I just wondered if some people have said that Bix got his style from-
And there was another kind of player like Don Murray.
Oh yeah, Don Murray.
And, uh-
Well, you said Steve Brown is probably the greatest bass player you said that you ever heard.
That's right. For me he is.
Yeah, he's wonderful. Those old Gold Cat records you can hear him.

He was the first guy to slobber around here. We had a guy with Ben Burnie. Ben Burnie was the MC, you know, that's when they're having those stage shows. So this Russian bass player is in the pit, see? So he says, uh, show me how Steve Brown slaps the bass. And I was like, boom, boom, boom, and slap back. So he's going down and he's playing an overture with Ben Burnie. And all of a sudden, in a quiet spot, this guy starts slapping the heck out of a bass and he breaks everybody up. He's supposed to do it there. He wanted to slap a bass like Steve Brown. There's another guy who plays good trumpet, Lou McGarrity.
Yeah.
Cutty Cutshall sounds good.
What about piano?
They made that album, Jimmy Dawson's, a very good Dixland album.
Yeah. I love that. What about the piano players in New Orleans? Were there many of them?
No, it was Williams, Joe Farrow, uh, well, I expect everyone to know, Williams, Farrow, and somebody else. Can't think of them.
Some of those early dance bands then you played but didn't even use piano.
That's right.
Did you ever play on a wagon to advertise?
Oh yeah, a lot. That's where they got the word tailgate from.
Yeah.

I was playing with Hodes at, I didn't know what it was all about. I'm playing with Hodes up at the Childs. Yeah. So they had a sign out there, Art Hodes needs Columbia Five feature in the King of the Tailgate, George Brunus. So I said to myself, what is this King of the Tailgate? What is this tailgate? So a guy come in and explain it to me. Why did they, because you sit on the tailgate of the wagon, you can't, you need more room to slide the slide. That's the way they do it. They set the drums up in front and then the trumpet and clarinet and the bass and trombone in the back.
Yeah. But you've never had that term applied to you down in New Orleans?
No.
You never called it that term?

You have to go places to learn other things. Oh, of course, we used to meet like Buddy Batiste, we'd be an advertiser of color dance, we'd be advertising dance, we'd meet on the same corner, we'd challenge each other. Then they'd put one direction, we'd go another direction, we'd play, get over dirty with the instrument, you know?
Oh yeah.
Then maybe an hour or so later we'd meet on another street, another corner.
Yeah. You heard Buddy Batiste, I never got to hear him, he didn't make any records either.
No.
Some people say he's as good as Louie.
I never heard Bunk Johnson down there, I never heard, what's this other guy, a Mark King of the Colors guy?
Well, I mean Joe Oliver down there.
Oh yeah.
And you heard him I guess when you were a kid.
And Henry Allen and Kepler.
I'm not sure, now that's what we have on that early tape, but I want to be sure about some of those, not dates necessary, but how old were you when you first took up music,
your alto horn you say? I was about five and a half, six years old.
Uh huh. And then how old were you when you got your first trombone? If you can remember, if not exactly, just about?
About ten.
About ten, and you didn't have long pants then of course?
No. That's the way bloomers with a uniform and a cap, you know, with Lane on the cap.
You got that trombone at a pawn shop you say?

No, well I didn't have the trombone until I played this date with, I was supposed to play upright alto that night. And Lane's brother-in-law didn't show up, lay on smallos, so the trombone was there, he says try to play the trombone.
That's when you first?
And after I liked the trombone, I went to the hawk shop and bought me one.
Yeah. That's crazy. And did you live down in that neighborhood all the time you lived in New Orleans until you moved up here?
2135, the house is still there, I was down there. Well still there. But in the neighborhood you wouldn't know it.
What's the number again?
2135 Roussau Street.
I'll take a picture of it sometime.
There's a corner store there now, there's two houses, second house.
Did any parades go through that territory much?

There was a trombone that dropped dead in front of my house. In the parade. In the car, you see they had the oyster shells, it was a sloppy street, so they're playing. Like they said in this book, this guy was playing, yeah, he makes a slide, he drops dead right in front of my house.
Right there, that's right.
And in this book, by General Martin's biography, it says this guy, Lucas says, or is it Dupaz, who wrote that biography, Dupaz or Lucas?
Lomax.
Lomax. Says that my greatest idol was Watson. I never heard of a Watson. Or Roy Palmer, was it? Oh yeah, Roy Palmer. Roy Palmer. I never heard of him.
No, he came up here pretty...
Did they say that was the guy that dropped dead in front of my house?
No, he's Roy Palmer, still living. I never heard of the guy.
I was going to send him a telegram, make him contradict that in some kind of way, because I never know the guy. My brother was my idol.
Yeah, I know, everybody should know that. That's why we're trying to get this interview, it's in your own words, so that...
If the guy was my idol, he'd have got credit for it, don't worry.
Yeah, I know.
Man, I used to drill when Henry played that slash pump.
Did they ever have any names like that for the trombone down there, like slash pump?
Well, you take the Dixieland tunes. Tiger Egg was called Number One. Dixieland, One Step was called Mutton Jeff. What? Yeah, and Sensation was called Meatballs.
Yeah, I've heard that.
And then nobody knows who wrote them to them. Dixieland came up here and they had them copyrighted and they claimed them.
I was going to say, we don't want to put you around here.
The only tune they wrote to me was Clarinet Marmalade. That wasn't played in the longs.
Shields, I guess, worked a lot on that, yeah.
Shields, Regas, and Morocco.
Well, I think we have just about everything we need, unless there's something else you'd like to add that you can think of, either about your life or your trombone style or playing.
For kids who want to take up instruments, lead a clean life. Get a lot of rest. And be good and polite to people. And you'll always get by. Stay away from the lush. That's all I can tell.
Okay, well, thanks very much, George. We certainly appreciate your advice and all your time in this story.
Of course, I don't practice what I preach, but for newcomers, it's a good idea.
Okay, thank you.

segments.title: Introduction and the telegram calling him to Chicago
segments.summary: Brunis introduces himself, gives his birth details, and tells how Rag Baby Stevens's wire brought Paul Mares and then him to Chicago and the Campbell Gardens.

segments.title: First snow, Blatt's Palm Garden and boxing with Muggsy
segments.summary: He plays the first set, goes wild in his first snow, meets Jack Pettis, Frank Snyder, Elmer Schoebel and Muggsy at Blatt's, and is made to box Muggsy; then the move to Lincoln Gardens and a Streckfus boat offer.

segments.title: Streckfus riverboat job and Rappolo joining the band
segments.summary: The band takes the boat job, Rappolo replaces the clarinetist at Davenport, and Bix sits in.

segments.title: Rappolo, Bee Palmer's act and the first band at Friars Inn
segments.summary: Brunis recalls Rappolo's girlfriend, Bee Palmer's shimmy act, and who made up the first band at Friars Inn.

segments.title: Personnel changes at Friars Inn: Stitzel, Pollack, Steve Brown
segments.summary: Schoebel and Snyder leave and are replaced by Mel Stitzel, Ben Pollack and Steve Brown, whom he calls the greatest jazz bassist.

segments.title: Ben Pollack sits in at Friars Inn
segments.summary: Pollack, hanging around with the Austin High kids, asks to sit in and impresses with his cymbal technique.

segments.title: What Friars Inn was like and the gangsters who came in
segments.summary: A basement place on Wabash owned by Mike Fritzel, popular with hoods and entertainers.

segments.title: Friars hours, Valentino Inn, and auditioning for Ted Lewis
segments.summary: After Friars he leads at the Valentino Inn, wins a Ted Lewis audition at the Apollo, dresses up for Broadway, and gets news of his mother's death.

segments.title: Getting Muggsy hired by Lewis; numerologist changes his name
segments.summary: He recommends Muggsy to Lewis, then in New York changes the spelling of his name on a numerologist's advice and tests it on Friday the 13th.

segments.title: Nick's in Greenwich Village and the Famous Door with Prima
segments.summary: He starts at Nick's, stays ten years, then forms the Famous Door group with Louis Prima and splits with him.

segments.title: Records made with Prima
segments.summary: A short exchange about the Prima records, one now reissued as a bootleg with Brunis as leader.

segments.title: Jimmy Ryan's and the move to Condon's
segments.summary: After the Mills Cavalcade he plays Jimmy Ryan's, then is hired at the Greenwich Village Condon's over Pesky's objections.

segments.title: Three years at Condon's and the Sky Club offer
segments.summary: Hackett vouches for him; he stays three years and then goes to Chicago's Sky Club with Scarsdale kids.

segments.title: Sky Club band quits; Blue Note, Jazz Limited and other Chicago jobs
segments.summary: His band leaves, forcing him to pay their fares, and he works the Blue Note with Hodes and others, then Jazz Limited.

segments.title: The 11-11 Club and other Chicago jobs from 1950
segments.summary: He dates his start at the 11-11 to June 1950 or 51 and lists his stints at the Red Arrow, Tom Tom and Preview.

segments.title: European tours with Ted Lewis
segments.summary: Three trips to France, England and Belgium with Lewis, playing Paris and London venues.

segments.title: Wow-wow mute and Patty Harmon
segments.summary: Lewis featured him on rhythm with the first wow-wow mute, made by Patty Harmon.

segments.title: Plungers, derbies, cans and other mute effects
segments.summary: Plunger on Lonesome Road, hats, molasses cans in New Orleans, Dave Kline's bulb, phonograph record in the bell.

segments.title: His King trombone
segments.summary: The first horn cost $3 at a pawn shop; his current King is some 47 years old and was refurbished once.

segments.title: Brother Henny and the stunts he originated
segments.summary: Brunis insists brother Henry was first to play with his foot and march on the Saints; he also tells of posing as a midget.

segments.title: The musical Brunis family and Papa Lane's Reliance band
segments.summary: Siblings' instruments, his father's after-dinner family sessions, and early dance jobs with Papa Lane.

segments.title: Young trombonists he has taught: Bobby Wright and Jimmy Butler
segments.summary: He praises the teenage Bobby Wright, urges kids to take up instruments instead of guns, and mentions Jimmy Butler.

segments.title: Never learning to read music
segments.summary: He took one lesson, was told his ear was too good, and feared reading after Henny died.

segments.title: Advice to young players and Ted Lewis as showman
segments.summary: Learn fundamentals then listen to records; Lewis taught him to talk to audiences; his own definition of Dixieland.

segments.title: Switching from upright alto to trombone
segments.summary: A missing trombonist in Pansy Lane's band led him to try the slide; positions came naturally.

segments.title: Tommy Dorsey's breathing control
segments.summary: He admires Tommy's breath control at the Paramount and speaks fondly of Jimmy.

segments.title: Never warming up or practicing
segments.summary: He plays cold off the street while others warm up, calling it a natural gift.

segments.title: First parades and the parks around New Orleans
segments.summary: Marching at age six on alto, playing snare for Tony Sbarbaro, and locating Gretna, Algiers, McDonoghville dance parks.

segments.title: Cousin Whitey who plays trombone with the jukebox
segments.summary: A cousin/nephew runs a corner saloon and plays trombone along with a jukebox.

segments.title: The undertaker's prank
segments.summary: Brunis tells how brother Abbie lay as a fake corpse to scare an embalmer.

segments.title: Abbie's building skills and bands in Biloxi
segments.summary: Talk about Abbie's handiwork and the Biloxi club scene.

segments.title: Growing up in the Irish Channel
segments.summary: The neighbourhood near Chapitoulas, lawn parties and brick fights with Basin Street.

segments.title: German family background
segments.summary: His grandfather came from Germany and the name is spelled Bruenies.

segments.title: Streetcar sightseeing band and playing the French Market
segments.summary: The brothers and Emmett Rogers play on a sightseeing car, earn tips and play for butchers.

segments.title: Fischer's band and prizefight advertising parades
segments.summary: Street bands advertising fights, drinks in bars, and the claim that alcohol stunted his growth.

segments.chapter: New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Tin Roof Blues
segments.title: Abbie's patched trombone, barbershop harmony and his view of the blues
segments.summary: Brothers' band harmony at Abby's house, and his theory that blues came from Jewish hymns plus African rhythm.

segments.chapter: New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Tin Roof Blues
segments.title: Tin Roof Blues: origin, publisher and copyright
segments.summary: Written as Rusty Rail Blues, retitled by Melrose, with royalties split among many names and a later renewal.

segments.chapter: New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Tin Roof Blues
segments.title: His Tin Roof Blues trombone chorus
segments.summary: He played what felt natural; everyone copies it, including Wingy's Tijuana trombonist.

segments.chapter: New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Tin Roof Blues
segments.title: Wingy Manone, In a Mood and money
segments.summary: He claims Wingy wrote the riff behind In the Mood and collected from Glenn Miller.

segments.chapter: New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Tin Roof Blues
segments.title: Leon Rappolo and Mike Fritzel
segments.summary: Rappolo's clarinet, his habits, the band's reading, and Fritzel's support for jazz.

segments.title: Playing at Milneburg camps
segments.summary: Weekend camp dances at the lake, where bands competed and he lost his slide.

segments.title: Bucktown and joining the union as a cymbal player
segments.summary: At Bruning's he got into the union at 16 or 17 on cymbals rather than trombone.

segments.title: Posing as the Dixieland band in Alexandria and waiting tables
segments.summary: Papa Lane's group copies Dixieland Jazz Band records, is run out of town, and he works in a restaurant.

segments.title: Identifying musicians in a photograph of Papa Lane's band
segments.summary: The interviewer and Brunis puzzle over Cardella, Reiner, and Ragas in the band picture.

segments.title: His father's hotel job and the family's cooking
segments.summary: His father supervised menus for Gulf hotels and was a baker; the brothers cook.

segments.title: The district and its closing
segments.summary: He marched through the district, recalls its closing, and again poses as a midget.

segments.title: Mardi Gras customs, brass bands and parade pay
segments.summary: Open house, segregated masks, cabarets passing the frying pan, Richie's cornet, band size and pay rates.

segments.title: Bore size, mouthpiece and imitating players
segments.summary: He uses a medium bore horn and a size 28 mouthpiece, and warns against copying equipment.

segments.title: Dixieland ensemble roles, tempos and set order
segments.summary: Trumpet lead, clarinet variations, trombone counter melody, drummer calls and march tempos.

segments.title: Slide cream, horn care and losing the trombone in New York
segments.summary: He uses cold cream and water on the slide and tells of losing the horn in a cab.

segments.title: Stage stunts and Henry's showmanship
segments.summary: His trombone-with-foot stunt, Henry's shimmying and jailing in Biloxi.

segments.title: Favorite trombone tone: Jerry Schrimmer and Murray McEachern
segments.summary: He names the finest tones he has heard, including his teacher.

segments.title: First recordings and the Mares dispute
segments.summary: Choosing a favorite, a Condon-era date, and the early NORK session with recording-horn problems.

segments.title: Marathon Ted Lewis session and the blues date with Spivak
segments.summary: Long Lewis takes with Jimmy Dorsey and a later blues session with Spivak and others.

segments.title: Lip trouble, embouchure and iron lip
segments.summary: A sore lip, advice on stomach and lip health, how he places the mouthpiece.

segments.title: Small dance bands with Papa Lane and a collapsed dance floor
segments.summary: Four-piece bands, no piano, and a hall floor that fell in at Harvey.

segments.title: Tom Brown's band and the Brown brothers' farmer costumes
segments.summary: The Brown brothers came to Chicago, Shields swapped jobs, and band members' trades.

segments.title: Paul Mares and playing with different trumpeters
segments.summary: Mares played well; a driving trumpet drives him; he avoids a bass.

segments.title: Larry Shields and other trombonists
segments.summary: Brief remarks on Shields, Schilling and trombonists on the coast.

segments.title: Teagarden's soft playing versus his own blasting and shading
segments.summary: Contrast of styles and learning dynamics late in life.

segments.title: Emmett Hardy and Bix
segments.summary: Hardy's talent, his illness, and comparison with Bix.

segments.title: Steve Brown's slap bass and other players
segments.summary: A bassist copies Steve Brown; remarks on trumpeters and New Orleans pianists.

segments.title: Wagon advertising and the tailgate trombone name
segments.summary: He learned the term tailgate in Chicago and explains its origin.

segments.title: Cutting contests with Buddy Petit and other Black bands
segments.summary: Wagon bands challenged each other; he did not hear Bunk Johnson or Oliver down there.

segments.title: Age at first alto and trombone, and the Roussel Street house
segments.summary: Alto at five and a half, trombone at about ten, and where he lived.

segments.title: Trombonist who dropped dead; disputing the Roy Palmer idol claim
segments.summary: He rejects Lomax's claim that Palmer was his idol; his brother Henry was.

segments.title: Nicknames for Dixieland tunes and who copyrighted them
segments.summary: Tunes had New Orleans names and were later claimed by the Dixieland band.

segments.title: Advice to young musicians and goodbye
segments.summary: Lead a clean life and stay away from drink; the interview closes.
